title: Show, don't tell
examples: How can I make my descriptions sound more exciting?
When I write about feelings, what should I focus on?
Can you give me examples of strong action verbs?

explain.say: Today we are learning to show instead of telling in our writing.
First we will look at using sensory detail in our writing.

items: Sight: The rain streaked down the window.
Sound: A sudden, loud crack echoed nearby.
Smell: The air smelled sharply of salt.

explain.say: Next we will focus on using strong actions instead of just naming things.
A good example of showing is describing fear using senses.

items: His palms sweated against the rough wood.
He could only hear the frantic thumping of his own heart.
A metallic taste filled his mouth.

explain.say: In real life, when you are describing a busy market, use all your senses.
A common mistake is telling the reader how someone feels directly.

faq.q: What is the difference between showing and telling?
faq.a: Telling is stating a fact directly to the reader. Showing is painting a picture using details so the reader feels it themselves.
asks: How do I make my writing more descriptive?
Should I just use adjectives all the time?

faq.q: How many senses should I try to include?
faq.a: You should try to use as many senses as possible to make the scene feel real. Sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch are all useful.
asks: Is it okay if I only use sight?
Do I need to use all five senses?

faq.q: Can I use strong verbs for emotions?
faq.a: Yes, strong verbs are excellent for showing action related to emotion. Instead of saying 'He was angry,' you can write 'He slammed the book shut.'
asks: What are some good verbs for fear?

faq.q: Does using too much detail slow down my story?
faq.a: It can if you include details that do not matter to the plot. Focus on details that reveal character or move the action forward.
asks: Should I describe everything I see?
How do I keep my descriptions moving?

faq.q: Is sensory detail only for nature scenes?
faq.a: No, you can use sensory detail anywhere. You can smell the old leather of a chair or hear the squeak of a floorboard indoors.
asks: Can I use smell in a city story?

facts: Sensory detail appeals to the five senses: sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Strong verbs are action words that create a clear picture of movement or speech.
Showing involves using concrete details to let the reader experience the scene.
Telling is summarizing an experience or emotion with simple statements.

quiz.say: When the character is nervous, which sentence shows this best?
quiz.show: Nervousness: A. He felt very scared. B. His hands trembled, and he kept wiping his sweaty palms.

options.show: B. His hands trembled, and he kept wiping his sweaty palms.
options.say: B. His hands trembled, and he kept wiping his sweaty palms.

options.show: C. He stared at the floor.
options.say: C. He stared at the floor.

options.show: D. He whispered a quick apology.
options.say: D. He whispered a quick apology.

quiz.why: This uses physical actions and touch (sweaty palms) to show the feeling, which is much stronger than just saying he felt scared.

wrong.1: This is telling because it labels the emotion directly to the reader.
wrong.2: This is okay, but it only uses sight, whereas the correct answer uses multiple senses and actions.
wrong.3: This only focuses on sound and doesn't capture the physical signs of nervousness.

quiz.say: Instead of saying 'The room was messy,' which sentence shows the messiness?
quiz.show: Messy Room: A. The room was messy. B. Clothes lay draped over the chair.

options.show: B. Clothes lay draped over the chair.
options.say: B. Clothes lay draped over the chair.

quiz.why: This uses a specific visual detail (clothes draped) to let the reader see the mess, which is better than the general word 'messy.'

wrong.0: This is too vague and does not give the reader a specific image to picture.
wrong.2: This is telling because it summarizes the state without giving details.
wrong.3: While this is a good detail, the correct option provides a more immediate and varied visual example.

quiz.say: To show excitement, which description works best?
quiz.show: Excitement: A. He was full of energy. B. He bounced across the lawn, chasing his own tail.

options.show: A. He was full of energy.
options.say: A. He was full of energy.

options.show: D. He tapped his foot rapidly.
options.say: D. He tapped his foot rapidly.

options.show: B. He bounced across the lawn, chasing his own tail.
options.say: B. He bounced across the lawn, chasing his own tail.

quiz.why: B uses strong action verbs ('bounced', 'chasing') and movement to let the reader feel the energy, rather than just stating it.

wrong.0: This is telling because it names the abstract feeling instead of showing the actions.
wrong.1: This only uses one sense (sight) and is not as dynamic as showing full physical action.
wrong.2: This is a good detail, but the correct answer shows a larger, more encompassing display of energy.
